description: Vital Link Orbita is a four-member family team united by a passion for health and space technologies. For NASA Space Apps Challenge Ankara, we are developing an intelligent system that continuously monitors astronauts’ health and helps detect potential risks early, supporting safer human space missions.
summary: LifeTether is a web app that helps an astronaut measure their own health, understand what the result means, and know what to do and who to tell. It tracks 34 health indicators. Most arrive automatically from simulated sensors and wearables; the rest are collected through five short game-like activities or entered manually. Each value is colour-coded by a rule with a named source, or compared with the astronaut's personal baseline. When a finding needs attention, the app shows three first steps, states who should know, and lets the astronaut notify the crew medical officer, who can forward it to the flight surgeon. Tethy, a voice agent, reads every record, answers questions aloud and navigates the app on command. This matters because the farther a crew travels, the longer a reply from Earth takes: up to 22 minutes one way on Mars. The first decision has to be made on board.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

LifeTether gathers health indicators, evaluates them, and guides the astronaut to a next step. It adapts to four mission modes (Orbit, Deep space, Moon, Mars) and three sub-contexts (habitat, rover, EVA).

HOW IT WORKS

1. Collect. 34 measurements, including the six named in the challenge (blood pressure, heart rate, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep, mood). Passive values come from simulated patches, wearables and cabin sensors. Active values come from five activities: Day Start (sleep, mood, symptoms, reaction time), Heart & Breath Break (heart rate, blood pressure, spirometry), Power Circuit (muscle strength), Senses Tour (vision, hearing, coordination) and Mission Fuel (nutrition by barcode). Points reward participation and a valid measurement, never the value.

2. Understand. A clickable body map and a dashboard show each value with a status colour. A value is coloured only when a referenced rule exists; otherwise it is shown against the personal baseline. Missing data stays "no data" and is never estimated. The app does not diagnose.

3. Act. A finding that needs attention shows three first steps (check the measurement, self-care, notify) and who should know. The astronaut can send that single measurement to the crew medical officer, who sees it in an inbox and can forward it to the flight surgeon. In Mars mode the app reminds the user of the communication delay.

4. Risks. A separate screen tracks 18 hazards grouped under NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight, and changes with the mission mode.

5. Tethy. A voice agent that talks with the astronaut in Turkish or English, summarises all records, opens the relevant screen on a voice command, sets reminders and, with approval, notifies the medical officer. It states numbers only from the record, does not diagnose or suggest medication, and stays silent during EVA unless addressed.

BENEFITS

Astronaut: self-assessment without waiting for the ground, and a clear next step.

Physician: only findings that need attention, each with value, status and comparison.

Mission: the crew can make the first decision on board when replies are delayed; the same software fits Orbit, Moon and Mars.

On Earth: the same pattern fits people who work far from a clinician (Antarctic stations, ships, mines) and patients monitored at home.

LIMITATIONS

All crew members, values and sensors are simulated. Most clinical ranges were written for Earth. The sensor mapping is a design assumption. Tethy uses a cloud language model in this prototype; a flight version would need an on-board model. If the model is unreachable, rule-based triggers and fixed replies keep working. The app's "Method & sources" page lists every rule with its source.

HOW TO TRY IT

Open the link, pick any crew profile and enter any four-digit PIN (sign-in is simulated; no account is needed). Use the EN/TR button to switch language.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript (ES modules, no build step); PHP proxy for API calls; Anthropic Claude API (language model with tool use); ElevenLabs text-to-speech; browser Web Speech API; GitHub and GitHub Actions for deployment.
dataRefs: NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) RadLab Data API: one day of measured absorbed dose rate from the DosTel1 detector in the ISS Columbus module (1 April 2022, 1,192 readings, averaged in 10-minute bins). Shown on the Risks screen in Orbit mode.
NASA-STD-3001 Volume 1, Appendix D: Requirements Compliance Matrix
NASA-STD-3001 Volume 2, Chapter 6: Natural and Induced Environments
Sanders et al. 2024, Inspiration4 data in NASA OSDR: sample types in the laboratory section
NASA-STD-3001 Volume 2, Chapter 7: Habitability Functions: energy intake comparison (3,035 kcal per crew member per day)
NASA OCHMO TB-004 Carbon Dioxide: cabin CO2 limit (one-hour average of no more than 3 mmHg)
NASA OCHMO TB-020 Ionizing Radiation Protection: career effective dose limit of 600 mSv
NASA OCHMO TB-027 Water – Human Consumption: fluid intake comparison (2.5 L of potable water per day); water around exercise and EVA
NASA OCHMO TB-041 Sleep Accommodations: background for the sleep rule and its limitation note
NASA HRP – The five hazards of human spaceflight: structure of the Risks screen (18 hazards in five groups)
NASA HRP – Human spaceflight risks: classification of hazards and health outcomes
NASA HRP – Gravity fields: gravity transition hazards and triggers
NASA – Risk of injury and compromised performance from EVA: symptom check after an EVA
NASA HHP – Risk of celestial dust exposure: dust hazards in Moon and Mars modes
NASA HHP – Bone and mineral evaluation: bone density entry and its limitation note
NASA HHP – Cardiovascular and vision: cardiovascular and vision entries
NASA – Brain fluid pressure: SANS entry on the Risks screen
NASA – Spaceflight Standard Measures: actigraphy combined with self-report in Day Start
NTRS 20200011570, JSC Fatigue Management Services: rest and sleep suggestions (naps, light, caffeine cut-off, sleep environment)
NASA TM 108839, planned rest: evidence for the short planned nap
NTRS 20190002008, sleep environment: cool, dark, quiet sleep station
NTRS 20205008023, Cognition and Fine Motor Skills batteries: touch coordination tasks in Senses Tour
NASA TechPort 23201, Psychomotor Vigilance Test on ISS: background for Reflex Hunt
Parisi et al. 2024, NASA Ames: communication delay of up to 22 minutes one way on Mars
projectRefs: ESA Columbus / DLR – DOSIS 3D experiment, DOSTEL detectors: the radiation series in the app was measured by the DOSTEL-1 detector of this DLR-led experiment in ESA's Columbus module (accessed through NASA OSDR RadLab)
CSA – Monitoring radiation for astronaut health: background for radiation monitoring design
DLR – CIMON-2 on the ISS: prior AI crew assistant; inspiration for Tethy
American Heart Association – All About Heart Rate: resting heart rate range
2025 AHA/ACC blood pressure guideline: blood pressure categories
2017 ACC/AHA hypertension guideline: first steps for a blood pressure finding
American Heart Association – Monitoring blood pressure at home: measurement flow in Heart & Breath Break
Royal College of Physicians, NEWS2: bands for respiratory rate, SpO2, systolic pressure, heart rate, temperature
AASM/SRS sleep consensus (2015): seven hours or more of sleep per night
American Diabetes Association, hypoglycemia levels: glucose thresholds of 70 and 54 mg/dL
Numeric Pain Rating Scale: cut-off points for the 0–10 pain scale
AAST end-tidal CO2 guideline: reference range of 35–45 mmHg
ATS/ERS spirometry standard (2019): acceptable and repeatable blows
U.S. FDA, pulse oximeter accuracy and limitations: first steps for an oxygen saturation finding
CDC fever definition (via Health Desk): fever threshold of 38.0 °C
CDC/NIOSH sleep tips: dim light and no screens before bed
Basner et al. 2011, PVT-B: three-minute reaction test; 500 ms lapse count
Åkerstedt and Gillberg 1990, Karolinska Sleepiness Scale: sleepiness self-report in Day Start
Samn and Perelli 1982, fatigue scale: fatigue self-report in Day Start
Drake et al. 2013, caffeine and sleep: caffeine cut-off suggestion
Anthropic Claude API: language model behind the Tethy agent
Web Speech API: voice input in the browser
Higgsfield: AI-generated character, icons, illustrations and fictional crew portraits
